claim: Thirty-three healthy participants performed a modified Sternberg task adapted to the auditory modality.
source: Thirty-three healthy participants performed a modified Sternberg task (Bonnefond and Jensen, 2012) adapted to the auditory modality.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design and participant count in the manuscript.

claim: Participants listened to a sequence of four consonants spoken by a female voice that had to be memorized across a 2-s retention period.
source: In each trial they listened to a sequence of four consonants spoken by a female voice (see Figure 1A). These items had to be memorized across a 2-s retention period, after which a probe item was presented.
evidence: This describes the experimental task design as shown in the text and Figure 1A.

claim: A distractor was presented precisely 2 s after onset of the last memory item.
source: Critically, precisely 2 s after onset of the last memory item, a distractor was presented that was either strong (a consonant spoken by a male voice) or weak (an acoustically scrambled version of a consonant).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the timing of distractor presentation in the experimental design.

claim: Strong distractors were consonants spoken by a male voice.
source: Critically, precisely 2 s after onset of the last memory item, a distractor was presented that was either strong (a consonant spoken by a male voice) or weak (an acoustically scrambled version of a consonant).
evidence: This directly describes the nature of strong distractors in the experimental design.

claim: Weak distractors were acoustically scrambled versions of consonants.
source: Critically, precisely 2 s after onset of the last memory item, a distractor was presented that was either strong (a consonant spoken by a male voice) or weak (an acoustically scrambled version of a consonant).
evidence: This directly describes the nature of weak distractors in the experimental design.

claim: Different distractor types were presented blockwise in a manner counterbalanced across participants.
source: The different distractor types were presented blockwise in a manner counterbalanced across participants.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for distractor presentation.

claim: Average accuracy was 85% for weak distractors and 83% for strong distractors.
source: Comparing average accuracy between the strong and the weak distractor conditions showed a small (85% vs 83%) but statistically significant (t32 = −2.11, pone-sided = 0.02; Cohen's d = 0.37, 'small effect') deterioration of performance for strong distractors.
evidence: This reports the measured behavioral accuracy data from the experiment.

claim: The difference in accuracy between strong and weak distractors was statistically significant (t32 = −2.11, pone-sided = 0.02; Cohen's d = 0.37).
source: Comparing average accuracy between the strong and the weak distractor conditions showed a small (85% vs 83%) but statistically significant (t32 = −2.11, pone-sided = 0.02; Cohen's d = 0.37, 'small effect') deterioration of performance for strong distractors.
evidence: This reports the statistical test results for the behavioral accuracy comparison.

claim: Reaction times were on average 9 ms slower for the strong distractor condition (579 ms vs 570 ms).
source: Reaction times were on average 9 ms slower for the strong distractor condition (579 ms vs 570 ms); however, this difference was not significant (t29 = 1.07, pone-sided = 0.14; Cohen's d = −0.20, 'very small effect').
evidence: This reports the measured reaction time data from the experiment.

claim: The difference in reaction times between strong and weak distractors was not statistically significant (t29 = 1.07, pone-sided = 0.14; Cohen's d = −0.20).
source: Reaction times were on average 9 ms slower for the strong distractor condition (579 ms vs 570 ms); however, this difference was not significant (t29 = 1.07, pone-sided = 0.14; Cohen's d = −0.20, 'very small effect').
evidence: This reports the statistical test results for the reaction time comparison.

claim: Response speed was not emphasized to avoid interference from button presses on processing of the probe item.
source: It should be noted that response speed was not emphasized to avoid interference from button presses on processing of the probe item.
evidence: This describes a methodological decision in the experimental design.

claim: The strong distractor condition was slightly more challenging than the weak distractor condition.
source: Overall, the behavioral analysis supports the notion that the strong distractor condition was slightly more challenging, laying a solid foundation for the subsequent MEG analysis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral results based on the accuracy data.

claim: Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) with 5-fold cross validation was used for temporal decoding.
source: To this end, we first applied temporal decoding, using linear discriminant analysis (LDA, 5-fold cross validation, repeated five times, AUC as a metric; see Figure 1A and 'Materials and methods' for details), on the post-probe MEG sensor-level activity, to classify whether a probe was part of the memory set or not.
evidence: This describes the analytical method used for decoding.

claim: Above-chance classification performance commenced ~334 ms after probe onset (pcluster = 4e-4).
source: The results are depicted in Figure 2A and show robust and sustained above-chance classification performance rapidly commencing ~334 ms after probe onset (pcluster = 4e-4) and lasting until the onset of the response prompt at 700 ms post-probe (Cohen's d in this period was generally >0.8, that is 'strong and very strong effects').
evidence: This reports the timing and statistical significance of the decoding results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Above-chance classification performance lasted until the onset of the response prompt at 700 ms post-probe.
source: The results are depicted in Figure 2A and show robust and sustained above-chance classification performance rapidly commencing ~334 ms after probe onset (pcluster = 4e-4) and lasting until the onset of the response prompt at 700 ms post-probe (Cohen's d in this period was generally >0.8, that is 'strong and very strong effects').
evidence: This reports the duration of above-chance decoding performance shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Cohen's d in the period of above-chance classification was generally >0.8.
source: The results are depicted in Figure 2A and show robust and sustained above-chance classification performance rapidly commencing ~334 ms after probe onset (pcluster = 4e-4) and lasting until the onset of the response prompt at 700 ms post-probe (Cohen's d in this period was generally >0.8, that is 'strong and very strong effects').
evidence: This reports the effect size for the decoding results.

claim: The time course of the decoding effect is in line with evoked response studies on old vs new effects in short-term memory.
source: The time course of this effect is very much in line with those seen in evoked response studies on old vs new effects in short-term memory (Danker et al., 2008; Kayser et al., 2003), indicating that early sensory activation is not informative on whether a probe was a memorized item or not.
evidence: This compares the current findings to previous literature.

claim: Early sensory activation is not informative on whether a probe was a memorized item or not.
source: The time course of this effect is very much in line with those seen in evoked response studies on old vs new effects in short-term memory (Danker et al., 2008; Kayser et al., 2003), indicating that early sensory activation is not informative on whether a probe was a memorized item or not.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the decoding results based on the timing of above-chance performance.

claim: A 0.4–0.7-s post-probe decoding period was used as a training set for time-generalized analysis.
source: In subsequent analyses, a 0.4–0.7-s post-probe decoding period was used as a training set, and the derived classifiers were applied in a time-generalized manner to the preceding retention period (yielding a quantitative proxy for the strength of memorized information; see below and also Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach for the time-generalized analysis.

claim: Time-generalized classifiers yield a quantitative proxy for the strength of memorized information.
source: In subsequent analyses, a 0.4–0.7-s post-probe decoding period was used as a training set, and the derived classifiers were applied in a time-generalized manner to the preceding retention period (yielding a quantitative proxy for the strength of memorized information; see below and also Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the time-generalized decoding approach.

claim: Informative Activity was derived in source space using an approach adapted from Marti and Dehaene, 2017.
source: In order to obtain insights into which brain regions may be contributing to the effect and aiding the identification of task-relevant region(s) in a data-driven manner (Jacquemot and Scott, 2006), we adapted an approach to derive Informative Activity in source space (Marti and Dehaene, 2017).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach for source localization, citing the original method.

claim: The approach projects sensor level classifier weights to source space using beamformer filters.
source: In brief, this approach projects the sensor level classifier weights to source space using beamformer filters.
evidence: This describes the technical details of the source localization method.

claim: A within-subject permutation analysis was implemented and classifier-weights were z-scored in a first-level analysis.
source: To make the effects more interpretable, we implemented a within-subject permutation analysis and z-scored the classifier-weights in a first-level analysis.
evidence: This describes the statistical approach used for the source analysis.

claim: A positive cluster (p=4e-4) was found at group-level when testing against zero using a nonparametric cluster permutation test.
source: These data were subsequently tested at group-level against zero within a nonparametric cluster permutation test using a t-test, yielding a positive cluster (p=4e-4) collapsed over the relevant post-probe time period.
evidence: This reports the statistical results of the group-level source analysis.

claim: Informative Activity was detected in widespread cortical regions encompassing temporal, parietal and frontal areas.
source: As shown in Figure 2A, Informative Activity can be detected in widespread cortical regions encompassing temporal, parietal and frontal areas.
evidence: This describes the spatial distribution of the source analysis results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The pattern of Informative Activity was bilateral with a clear left-hemispheric dominance.
source: Although the pattern was bilateral, there was a clear left-hemispheric dominance, with the most pronounced effect localizable to lSTG.
evidence: This describes the lateralization pattern observed in the source analysis.

claim: The most pronounced effect was localizable to left superior temporal gyrus (lSTG).
source: Although the pattern was bilateral, there was a clear left-hemispheric dominance, with the most pronounced effect localizable to lSTG.
evidence: This identifies the primary region of interest from the source analysis.

claim: Left superior temporal gyrus is particularly involved in processing speech sounds.
source: Given the particular involvement of this latter area in processing speech sounds (e.g. Mesgarani et al., 2014; see also Billig et al., 2019) and its central role in phonological short-term memory (Jacquemot and Scott, 2006), it was used as a task-relevant region of interest for the spectral analysis (see below).
evidence: This cites previous literature to support the functional role of lSTG.

claim: Left superior temporal gyrus has a central role in phonological short-term memory.
source: Given the particular involvement of this latter area in processing speech sounds (e.g. Mesgarani et al., 2014; see also Billig et al., 2019) and its central role in phonological short-term memory (Jacquemot and Scott, 2006), it was used as a task-relevant region of interest for the spectral analysis (see below).
evidence: This cites previous literature to support the functional role of lSTG in memory.

claim: lSTG was used as a task-relevant region of interest for the spectral analysis.
source: Given the particular involvement of this latter area in processing speech sounds (e.g. Mesgarani et al., 2014; see also Billig et al., 2019) and its central role in phonological short-term memory (Jacquemot and Scott, 2006), it was used as a task-relevant region of interest for the spectral analysis (see below).
evidence: This describes the methodological decision to focus on lSTG for subsequent analyses.

claim: The strongest classification results in time generalization were obtained approximately at the onset of the target (at 2 s).
source: Trivially, the strongest classification results are obtained approximately at the onset of the target (at 2 s), which corresponds to the area close to the diagonal of the time generalization matrix.
evidence: This describes the pattern observed in the time generalization analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: For the late 0.4–0.7-s post-probe training time period, decoding accuracy gradually ramps up over the retention interval.
source: It is evident that for the late 0.4–0.7-s post-probe training time period (probe onset at 2 s shown on the y-axis), decoding accuracy gradually ramps up over the retention interval.
evidence: This describes the temporal pattern of decoding accuracy in the time generalization analysis.

claim: Statistical analysis yielded two peak effects at ~400 ms and ~200 ms preceding the distractor onset.
source: This analysis yielded two peak effects at ~400 ms and ~200 ms (Cohen's d in these periods ~0.6 and ~0.55, respectively, that is, medium effect sizes) preceding the distractor onset, during which critical t-values (±2.0369) were exceeded.
evidence: This reports the timing of peak effects in the statistical comparison between conditions.

claim: Cohen's d in the periods of peak effects was ~0.6 and ~0.55, respectively.
source: This analysis yielded two peak effects at ~400 ms and ~200 ms (Cohen's d in these periods ~0.6 and ~0.55, respectively, that is, medium effect sizes) preceding the distractor onset, during which critical t-values (±2.0369) were exceeded.
evidence: This reports the effect sizes for the peak differences between conditions.

claim: Only the difference at ~200 ms preceding distractor onset was significant following a nonparametric permutation test (pcluster = 0.0156).
source: However, only the latter difference was significant following a nonparametric permutation test (pcluster = 0.0156).
evidence: This reports the statistical significance of the comparison between conditions.

claim: Memorized information is differentially activated prior to distractor onset, with relatively reduced activation prior to the strong distractor.
source: These results suggest that memorized information is differentially activated prior to distractor onset, with relatively reduced activation prior to the strong distractor.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the time-generalized decoding results.

claim: Average decoding accuracy prior to the strong distractor was significantly below chance (t32 = −3.98, p=3.63e-04).
source: In fact, when post-hoc testing the decoding accuracy over the entire test- and training-time window, average decoding accuracy prior to the strong distractor was significantly below chance (t32 = −3.98, p=3.63e-04), whereas it did not differ for weak distractors (t32 = −1.73, p=0.09).
evidence: This reports the statistical test results for decoding accuracy prior to strong distractors.

claim: Average decoding accuracy prior to weak distractors did not differ from chance (t32 = −1.73, p=0.09).
source: In fact, when post-hoc testing the decoding accuracy over the entire test- and training-time window, average decoding accuracy prior to the strong distractor was significantly below chance (t32 = −3.98, p=3.63e-04), whereas it did not differ for weak distractors (t32 = −1.73, p=0.09).
evidence: This reports the statistical test results for decoding accuracy prior to weak distractors.

claim: Below-chance decoding is not uncommon in time- and condition-generalization decoding approaches.
source: Below-chance decoding may appear surprising but is not uncommon in time- and condition-generalization decoding approaches (King and Dehaene, 2014).
evidence: This cites previous literature to contextualize the below-chance decoding result.

claim: Below-chance decoding translates into a systematic relative absence of memory-item specific patterns akin to those elicited during relevant periods following probe onset.
source: Although the precise neural processes leading to these patterns are challenging to pinpoint, in functional terms, this result translates into a systematic relative absence of memory-item specific patterns akin to those elicited during relevant periods following probe onset.
evidence: This provides a functional interpretation of the below-chance decoding result.

claim: Some representation with regards to the memorized item would need to be present during the periods of below chance decoding.
source: As this activation gradually ramps up toward the anticipated onset of the probe in both conditions, albeit somewhat delayed in the strong distractor condition, it is clear that some representation with regards to the memorized item would also need to be present during the periods of below chance decoding.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the pattern of decoding results across time.

claim: Network-level 'activity silent' processes encoding working memory content have been described by Stokes, 2015 and Wolff et al., 2017.
source: Recently, Stokes, 2015 and Wolff et al., 2017 described network-level 'activity silent' processes encoding working memory content, and similar processes could be present in the early part of the retention period in the present task.
evidence: This cites previous literature on activity-silent working memory processes.

claim: Similar activity-silent processes could be present in the early part of the retention period in the present task.
source: Recently, Stokes, 2015 and Wolff et al., 2017 described network-level 'activity silent' processes encoding working memory content, and similar processes could be present in the early part of the retention period in the present task.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation linking previous findings to the current results.

claim: The decoding effect is in line with the behavioral results, implying an overall detrimental impact associated with anticipation of a strong distractor.
source: Overall, the described decoding effect is in line with the behavioral results described above, implying an overall detrimental impact associated with anticipation of a strong distractor.
evidence: This connects the decoding results to the behavioral findings.

claim: Time-frequency representations show strong ongoing alpha/beta activity with a peak ~10 Hz in the lSTG.
source: The time-frequency representations in Figure 3A, which display the induced power in the 5–25 Hz range, show strong ongoing alpha/beta activity with a peak ~10 Hz in the lSTG.
evidence: This describes the spectral characteristics observed in Figure 3A.

claim: An alpha power decrease was observed in the strong as compared with the weak distractor condition in the 500-ms period preceding the distractor.
source: Analogous to the study by Bonnefond and Jensen, 2012, a 500-ms period preceding the occurrence of the distractor is marked, suggesting an alpha power decrease in the strong as compared with the weak distractor condition.
evidence: This describes the pattern observed in the time-frequency analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A nonparametric permutation test yielded a significant difference (pcluster = 0.0104) in the pre-distractor period.
source: This impression is supported by a nonparametric permutation test (pcluster = 0.0104), which yields a significant difference in this period with peak differences of ~12–13 Hz and ~21–22 Hz (Figure 3A, right panel), comparable to those recorded in the study in the visual domain (Bonnefond and Jensen, 2012).
evidence: This reports the statistical significance of the power difference between conditions.

claim: Peak differences were observed at ~12–13 Hz and ~21–22 Hz.
source: This impression is supported by a nonparametric permutation test (pcluster = 0.0104), which yields a significant difference in this period with peak differences of ~12–13 Hz and ~21–22 Hz (Figure 3A, right panel), comparable to those recorded in the study in the visual domain (Bonnefond and Jensen, 2012).
evidence: This reports the frequency ranges showing the largest power differences.

claim: The peak differences are comparable to those recorded in the visual domain study by Bonnefond and Jensen, 2012.
source: This impression is supported by a nonparametric permutation test (pcluster = 0.0104), which yields a significant difference in this period with peak differences of ~12–13 Hz and ~21–22 Hz (Figure 3A, right panel), comparable to those recorded in the study in the visual domain (Bonnefond and Jensen, 2012).
evidence: This compares the current findings to previous literature in the visual modality.

claim: Clear post-distractor evoked alpha enhancements could be observed.
source: However, even though clear post-distractor evoked alpha enhancements could be observed (see Figure 3B), no prominent evoked alpha could be observed preceding the distractor (an analysis using ITC leads to an identical conclusion; data not shown).
evidence: This describes the evoked power pattern shown in Figure 3B.

claim: No prominent evoked alpha could be observed preceding the distractor.
source: However, even though clear post-distractor evoked alpha enhancements could be observed (see Figure 3B), no prominent evoked alpha could be observed preceding the distractor (an analysis using ITC leads to an identical conclusion; data not shown).
evidence: This describes the absence of pre-distractor evoked alpha in Figure 3B.

claim: An analysis using inter-trial coherence (ITC) leads to an identical conclusion regarding the absence of pre-distractor evoked alpha.
source: However, even though clear post-distractor evoked alpha enhancements could be observed (see Figure 3B), no prominent evoked alpha could be observed preceding the distractor (an analysis using ITC leads to an identical conclusion; data not shown).
evidence: This reports an additional analysis confirming the absence of pre-distractor phase alignment.

claim: The statistical test for evoked power showed no difference at the cluster corrected level.
source: For the sake of completeness, we ran an analogous statistical test as for the induced power, showing no difference at the cluster corrected level (Figure 3B, right panel).
evidence: This reports the statistical results for the evoked power comparison.

claim: No evidence was found that auditory cortical alpha phase is adjusted in a top-down manner.
source: This result extends a previous report (van Diepen et al., 2015) in finding no evidence that auditory cortical alpha phase is adjusted in a top-down manner.
evidence: This interprets the absence of pre-distractor evoked alpha in the context of previous literature.

claim: Trials were sorted according to alpha (13 ± 3 Hz) or beta (21 ± 3 Hz) power in lSTG in a 400–1000-ms time period following the onset of the retention period.
source: To address the functional relevance of pre-distractor alpha and beta power modulations in the lSTG in greater detail, trials were sorted according to alpha (13 ± 3 Hz) or beta (21 ± 3 Hz) power in this region in a 400–1000-ms time period following the onset of the retention period (i.e. a 600-ms pre-distractor window centered on peak latency effect at 700 ms).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach for the power-binning analysis.

claim: Trials were median split into high and low alpha or beta power bins.
source: Subsequently, these trials were median split into high and low alpha or beta power bins.
evidence: This describes the binning procedure for the power analysis.

claim: A repeated measures ANOVA showed that the strength of memorized information did not differ overall between the frequency bands (F1,32 = 1.19, p=0.28).
source: To test for overall differences in the strength of memorized information between low- and high-power bins we first ran a repeated measures ANOVA using frequency band (alpha and beta) and bin (high and low) as factors. This analysis showed that the strength of memorized information did not differ overall between the frequency bands (F1,32 = 1.19, p=0.28).
evidence: This reports the statistical results for the main effect of frequency band.

claim: A trend was observed for bins (F1,32 = 3.29, p=0.08) with low-power bins showing relatively increased strength of memorized information.
source: A trend was observed for bins (F1,32 = 3.29, p=0.08) with low-power bins showing relatively increased strength of memorized information (see Figure 4A).
evidence: This reports the statistical results for the main effect of power bins.

claim: The interaction effect (F1,32 = 4.06, p=0.05) indicated that the difference between bins was not uniform for the alpha and beta bands.
source: However, the interaction effect (F1,32 = 4.06, p=0.05) indicated that this difference was not uniform for the alpha and beta bands.
evidence: This reports the statistical results for the interaction between frequency band and power bin.

claim: A difference in strength of memorized information was only significant for beta (t32 = 2.27, p=0.03) and not for alpha (t32 = 0.06, p=0.95).
source: Comparing strength of memorized information within each frequency band showed that a difference was only significant for beta (t32 = 2.27, p=0.03) and not for alpha (t32 = 0.06, p=0.95).
evidence: This reports the statistical results for the planned comparisons within each frequency band.

claim: Overall pre-distractor power in the beta frequency range in lSTG goes along with relatively increased strength of memorized information, in line with a prioritization account.
source: Thus, in line with a prioritization account (see Figure 1B), overall pre-distractor power in the beta frequency range in lSTG goes along with relatively increased strength of memorized information.
evidence: This interprets the beta power results in the context of the prioritization account.

claim: Modulations between low- and high-power trials were significantly stronger for alpha oscillations as compared to beta oscillations (t32 = 3.11, p=0.004).
source: In this respect, an interesting first observation is that modulations between low- and high-power trials (computed in each participant as the log10 ratio between high and low power trials in the relevant band) were significantly stronger for alpha oscillations as compared to beta oscillations (t32 = 3.11, p=0.004; compare also Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This reports the statistical comparison of power modulation extent between frequency bands.

claim: Correlating power modulation with differences in strength of memorized information yielded a significant effect only for alpha oscillations (r = −0.36, p=0.04).
source: Correlating this power modulation measure with the differences in strength of memorized information between low- and high-power trials yielded a significant effect only for alpha oscillations (alpha — r = −0.36, p=0.04; beta — r = 0.06, p=0.72), a pattern that better fits a prioritization account (see Figure 1B).
evidence: This reports the correlation results for alpha oscillations.

claim: Correlating power modulation with differences in strength of memorized information showed no significant effect for beta oscillations (r = 0.06, p=0.72).
source: Correlating this power modulation measure with the differences in strength of memorized information between low- and high-power trials yielded a significant effect only for alpha oscillations (alpha — r = −0.36, p=0.04; beta — r = 0.06, p=0.72), a pattern that better fits a prioritization account (see Figure 1B).
evidence: This reports the correlation results for beta oscillations.

claim: For alpha, the correlation effect is driven by the high-power trials.
source: A follow-up correlation analysis on the separate bins shows that for alpha this effect is driven by the high-power trials (Figure 4B).
evidence: This reports the results of a follow-up analysis examining which bin drives the correlation.

claim: Relatively desynchronized states in the alpha and beta bands appear to go along with relatively increased strength of memorized information, which is in accordance with a prioritization process.
source: Altogether, relatively desynchronized states in the alpha and beta bands appear to go along with relatively increased strength of memorized information, which is in accordance with a prioritization process.
evidence: This is an overall interpretation of the power-binning results.

claim: Beta desynchronization appears to prioritize memorized information in general.
source: Beta desynchronization appears to prioritize memorized information in general, whereas the alpha processes seem to be dependent on individually varying modulations.
evidence: This is an interpretation distinguishing the functional roles of alpha and beta.

claim: Alpha processes seem to be dependent on individually varying modulations.
source: Beta desynchronization appears to prioritize memorized information in general, whereas the alpha processes seem to be dependent on individually varying modulations.
evidence: This is an interpretation distinguishing the functional roles of alpha and beta.

claim: The basic decoding was repeated following filtering of the data in different frequency bands (broadband — 1–30 Hz; theta — 1–7 Hz; alpha — 9–17 Hz; beta — 18–24 Hz).
source: For this purpose, the basic decoding shown in Figure 1A, that is whether a probe was part of a memory set or not, was repeated following filtering of the data in different frequency bands (broadband — 1–30 Hz; theta — 1–7 Hz; alpha — 9–17 Hz; beta — 18–24 Hz) and by either applying the Hilbert transform or not.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach for the frequency-resolved decoding analysis.

claim: Decoding was poor for the alpha and beta bands in general.
source: Importantly for the purpose of addressing the potential circularity issue, decoding was poor for the alpha and beta bands in general (see Figure 5A), and did not differ from chance for the relevant time period upon which our time-generalized effects are based (see Figure 5B).
evidence: This reports the results of the frequency-resolved decoding analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Decoding did not differ from chance for the alpha and beta bands for the relevant 0.4–0.7-s post-probe time period.
source: Importantly for the purpose of addressing the potential circularity issue, decoding was poor for the alpha and beta bands in general (see Figure 5A), and did not differ from chance for the relevant time period upon which our time-generalized effects are based (see Figure 5B).
evidence: This reports the results for the specific time period used in the main analysis.

claim: For the broadband analysis, decoding was significantly above chance when using only the analytic amplitude part following the Hilbert transform (t32 = 4.19, p=0.0002).
source: For the broadband analysis, decoding was also significantly above chance when using only the analytic amplitude part following the Hilbert transform (t32 = 4.19, p=0.0002), although this is significantly lower than when using the original broadband signal (t32 = −6.22, p=5.68e–07).
evidence: This reports the statistical results for broadband decoding using analytic amplitude.

claim: Broadband decoding using analytic amplitude was significantly lower than when using the original broadband signal (t32 = −6.22, p=5.68e–07).
source: For the broadband analysis, decoding was also significantly above chance when using only the analytic amplitude part following the Hilbert transform (t32 = 4.19, p=0.0002), although this is significantly lower than when using the original broadband signal (t32 = −6.22, p=5.68e–07).
evidence: This reports the statistical comparison between different signal representations for broadband.

claim: A similar pattern can be observed for the theta band, with significant above-chance decoding for the real (t32 = 9.62, p=5.78e-11) and analytic amplitude (t32 = 6.26, p=5.11e-07) versions of the signal.
source: A similar pattern can be observed for the theta band, with significant above-chance decoding for the real (t32 = 9.62, p=5.78e-11) and analytic amplitude (t32 = 6.26, p=5.11e-07) versions of the signal (for real vs analytic amplitude, t32 = −4.80, p=3.25e–05).
evidence: This reports the statistical results for theta band decoding.

claim: For theta band, decoding using the real signal was significantly better than using analytic amplitude (t32 = −4.80, p=3.25e–05).
source: A similar pattern can be observed for the theta band, with significant above-chance decoding for the real (t32 = 9.62, p=5.78e-11) and analytic amplitude (t32 = 6.26, p=5.11e-07) versions of the signal (for real vs analytic amplitude, t32 = −4.80, p=3.25e–05).
evidence: This reports the statistical comparison between signal representations for theta band.

claim: Decoding when using only the theta band was overall superior as compared to that using the broadband signal (real signal — t32 = 10.71, p=4.10e–12; analytic amplitude — t32 = 7.11, p=4.53e–08).
source: Decoding when using only the theta band was overall superior as compared to that using the broadband signal (real signal — t32 = 10.71, p=4.10e–12; analytic amplitude — t32 = 7.11, p=4.53e–08).
evidence: This reports the statistical comparison between theta and broadband decoding.

claim: Alpha/beta band modulations do not appear to carry actual (decodable) information about the memorized item.
source: To summarize: alpha/beta band modulations, which are different on average prior to strong and weak distractors, do not appear to carry actual (decodable) information about the memorized item (see also Griffiths et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the frequency-resolved decoding results.

claim: The most important signal component contributing to the analysis is in the theta frequency range.
source: The most important signal component contributing to our analysis (Figure 1A) is in the theta frequency range.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the frequency-resolved decoding results.

claim: The temporal fine structure, as compared to simple amplitude modulations, seems to contain relevant representational information.
source: Interestingly, the temporal fine structure, as compared to simple amplitude modulations, seems to contain relevant representational information.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the comparison between real and Hilbert-transformed signals.

claim: The behavioral effects are weaker than in the original visual experiment by Bonnefond and Jensen, 2012.
source: The behavioral effects are weaker than in the original visual experiment by Bonnefond and Jensen, 2012.
evidence: This compares the current behavioral results to those from the cited study.

claim: Alpha/beta power prior to the presentation of the strong distractor decreased, whereas it was relatively sustained in the weak distractor condition.
source: Interestingly, alpha/beta power prior to the presentation of the strong distractor decreased, whereas it was relatively sustained in the weak distractor condition.
evidence: This summarizes the main spectral finding from the induced power analysis.

claim: This effect is at odds with findings reported in the visual modality using an analogous paradigm.
source: This effect is at odds with findings reported in the visual modality using an analogous paradigm (Bonnefond and Jensen, 2012), where — in line with idea of an inhibitory role for alpha oscillations (Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010; Klimesch et al., 2007) — induced alpha/beta enhancements were seen prior to a strong distractor.
evidence: This compares the current findings to those from the visual modality study.

claim: In the Bonnefond and Jensen study, induced alpha/beta enhancements were seen prior to a strong distractor.
source: This effect is at odds with findings reported in the visual modality using an analogous paradigm (Bonnefond and Jensen, 2012), where — in line with idea of an inhibitory role for alpha oscillations (Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010; Klimesch et al., 2007) — induced alpha/beta enhancements were seen prior to a strong distractor.
evidence: This describes the findings from the cited visual modality study.

claim: The induced power effect in the Bonnefond and Jensen study was broadband and included the beta frequency range.
source: As in our study, the induced power effect in the Bonnefond and Jensen study was broadband and thus included the beta frequency range (see Figure 2 in Bonnefond and Jensen, 2012), although these authors focused only on the alpha (8–12 Hz) parts in their follow-up analysis.
evidence: This describes the spectral characteristics of the findings in the cited study.

claim: Both alpha and beta powers are relevant in a seemingly differential manner with respect to prioritization of memorized information.
source: Our follow-up analysis, however, shows that both alpha and beta powers are relevant in a seemingly differential manner with respect to prioritization of memorized information.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current study's findings regarding alpha and beta.

claim: Pronounced pre-distractor evoked alpha power effects were observed in the Bonnefond and Jensen study.
source: In the Bonnefond and Jensen study, pronounced pre-distractor evoked alpha power effects were observed that could not be identified in our auditory task.
evidence: This describes a finding from the cited study that was not replicated in the current study.

claim: Pre-distractor evoked alpha power effects could not be identified in the current auditory task.
source: In the Bonnefond and Jensen study, pronounced pre-distractor evoked alpha power effects were observed that could not be identified in our auditory task.
evidence: This describes a negative finding in the current study.

claim: This negative finding could be modality specific.
source: This negative finding could be modality specific but does also fit well with recent reported problems in identifying attentional pre-stimulus alpha-phase adjustment (van Diepen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the negative finding regarding evoked alpha.

claim: The negative finding fits well with recent reported problems in identifying attentional pre-stimulus alpha-phase adjustment.
source: This negative finding could be modality specific but does also fit well with recent reported problems in identifying attentional pre-stimulus alpha-phase adjustment (van Diepen et al., 2015).
evidence: This contextualizes the negative finding with other literature.

claim: Desynchronization in both alpha and beta frequency ranges appears to prioritize representations as suggested by other frameworks.
source: Overall, while desynchronization in both frequency ranges appears to prioritize representations as suggested by other frameworks (Hanslmayr et al., 2016; van Ede, 2018), our results suggest functionally distinct contributions by auditory cortical alpha and beta oscillations.
evidence: This interprets the current findings in the context of existing theoretical frameworks.

claim: The results suggest functionally distinct contributions by auditory cortical alpha and beta oscillations.
source: Overall, while desynchronization in both frequency ranges appears to prioritize representations as suggested by other frameworks (Hanslmayr et al., 2016; van Ede, 2018), our results suggest functionally distinct contributions by auditory cortical alpha and beta oscillations.
evidence: This is a key conclusion from the current study.

claim: The extent to which alpha power was modulated within participants was significantly stronger than that for beta.
source: Interestingly, the extent to which alpha power was modulated within participants was significantly stronger than that for beta.
evidence: This reports a comparison of modulation extent between frequency bands.

claim: The study underlines the value of combining conventional spectral analysis approaches with multi-voxel pattern analysis (MVPA) in advancing our understanding of the functional role of brain oscillations in the auditory system.
source: Altogether, our study underlines the value of combining conventional spectral analysis approaches with multi-voxel pattern analysis (MVPA) in advancing our understanding of the functional role of brain oscillations in the auditory system.
evidence: This is a methodological conclusion about the value of the combined analytical approach.

claim: Alpha enhancements in challenging listening tasks have been linked to the selective inhibition of irrelevant 'channels' of auditory information.
source: In line with dominant views regarding the functional relevance of alpha oscillations (Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010; Klimesch et al., 2007), alpha enhancements in such circumstances have been linked to the selective inhibition of irrelevant 'channels' of auditory information (Strauß et al., 2014).
evidence: This cites previous literature on the functional role of alpha in auditory tasks.

claim: A large proportion of studies illustrating enhanced task-related alpha power are based on manipulation of selective attention.
source: In terms of tasks, a large proportion of studies illustrating enhanced task-related alpha power are not fully comparable to the present study because they are based on manipulation of selective attention (Fu et al., 2001; Worden et al., 2000) or on the processing of degraded (and thus more challenging) speech (but see alternative studies showing alpha decreases to track increased speech degradation, for example McMahon et al., 2016 and Miles et al., 2017; see also Hauswald et al., 2019).
evidence: This contextualizes the current study within the broader literature on alpha power.

claim: Some studies reported the functional relevance of alpha enhancements during retention periods of auditory working memory tasks.
source: Some studies also reported the functional relevance of alpha enhancements during retention periods of auditory working memory tasks (e.g. Obleser et al., 2012; Wilsch et al., 2015), but these studies did not introduce strong/weak distractors at predictable time points.
evidence: This cites previous literature on alpha in auditory working memory.

claim: Previous auditory working memory studies did not introduce strong/weak distractors at predictable time points.
source: Some studies also reported the functional relevance of alpha enhancements during retention periods of auditory working memory tasks (e.g. Obleser et al., 2012; Wilsch et al., 2015), but these studies did not introduce strong/weak distractors at predictable time points.
evidence: This distinguishes the current study design from previous auditory working memory studies.

claim: The sources of alpha enhancement effects have most frequently been identified in non-auditory brain regions.
source: Importantly, however, the sources of these alpha enhancement effects have most frequently been identified in non-auditory brain regions (e.g. Obleser and Weisz, 2012; Wilsch et al., 2015) and rarely in the auditory cortex (e.g. Müller and Weisz, 2012).
evidence: This summarizes the typical source localization findings from previous literature.

claim: Reduction of auditory cortical alpha activity has been commonly linked to attended as well as perceived (including illusory) auditory input.
source: Indeed, reduction of auditory cortical alpha activity has been commonly linked to attended (Frey et al., 2014) as well as perceived (including illusory) auditory input (e.g. Leske et al., 2014; Müller et al., 2013; Weisz et al., 2007; Billig et al., 2019; for a more general perspective see Lange et al., 2014).
evidence: This cites previous literature on auditory cortical alpha reductions.

claim: The association of alpha modulations to attended/ignored or perceived auditory information has to date been very indirect.
source: The association of alpha modulations to attended/ignored or perceived auditory information has to date been very indirect.
evidence: This characterizes the state of previous research on alpha and auditory information.

claim: The study significantly advances the state by showing a relationship between alpha/beta power in the left auditory cortex and strength of memorized information in the retention period.
source: Our study significantly advances this state by showing a relationship between alpha/beta power in the left auditory cortex and strength of memorized information in the retention period.
evidence: This is a claim about the contribution of the current study to the field.

claim: This result supports the interpretations of studies showing alpha power reductions in the auditory modality.
source: This result supports the interpretations of studies showing alpha power reductions in the auditory modality and a more general assertion that cortical alpha/beta desynchronization during memory tasks represents the content of memorized information (Hanslmayr et al., 2016).
evidence: This connects the current findings to previous literature on alpha reductions.

claim: Cortical alpha/beta desynchronization during memory tasks represents the content of memorized information.
source: This result supports the interpretations of studies showing alpha power reductions in the auditory modality and a more general assertion that cortical alpha/beta desynchronization during memory tasks represents the content of memorized information (Hanslmayr et al., 2016).
evidence: This cites a theoretical framework about the role of alpha/beta desynchronization.

claim: Similar to a recent fMRI study using a representational similarity approach, suppression of alpha/beta power itself does not carry the information content but is likely to be a process that enables this to occur.
source: Similar to a recent fMRI study using a representational similarity approach (Griffiths et al., 2019), we show that suppression of alpha/beta power itself does not carry the information content but is likely to be a process that enables this to occur.
evidence: This compares the current findings to a recent fMRI study and interprets the role of alpha/beta power.

claim: Content-specific information appears to be largely driven by slow (delta/theta) activity.
source: In our study, which used broadband signals in a first step of the decoding analysis, this content-specific information appears to be largely driven by slow (delta/theta) activity, with the temporal fine structure containing relevant information on top of the slower amplitude changes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the frequency-resolved decoding results.

claim: The temporal fine structure contains relevant information on top of the slower amplitude changes.
source: In our study, which used broadband signals in a first step of the decoding analysis, this content-specific information appears to be largely driven by slow (delta/theta) activity, with the temporal fine structure containing relevant information on top of the slower amplitude changes.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the comparison between real and Hilbert-transformed signals.

claim: The results can be reconciled with those of previous studies focusing on alpha enhancements in auditory tasks, as alpha reductions or enhancements may show engagements of different neural systems in processing relevant or blocking irrelevant information, respectively.
source: Overall, our results can be reconciled with those of previous studies focusing on alpha enhancements in auditory tasks, as alpha reductions or enhancements may show engagements of different neural systems in processing relevant or blocking irrelevant information, respectively (van Ede, 2018).
evidence: This provides a theoretical framework for reconciling the current findings with previous literature.

claim: The functional versatility of alpha power modulations in listening tasks serves as a precaution not to equate alpha power enhancements simplistically to concepts such as listening effort.
source: The functional versatility of alpha power modulations in listening tasks also serves as a precaution not to equate, for example, alpha power enhancements simplistically to concepts such as listening effort (McGarrigle et al., 2014; Pichora-Fuller et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a cautionary interpretation about the functional interpretation of alpha power.

claim: Precise predictability of the occurrence of an auditory distractor leads to an anticipatory prioritization of memorized information.
source: In summary, precise predictability of the occurrence of an auditory distractor leads to an anticipatory prioritization of memorized information.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study.

claim: Modulations of alpha/beta oscillations in task-relevant auditory cortical regions could be a relevant process mediating the 'protection' of relevant auditory information against interference.
source: We show that modulations of alpha/beta oscillations in task-relevant auditory cortical regions could be a relevant process mediating the 'protection' of relevant auditory information against interference.
evidence: This is a key conclusion about the functional role of alpha/beta oscillations.

claim: The results suggest a somewhat differential and to date unreported pattern for alpha and beta frequency ranges in the auditory system.
source: Interestingly, our results suggest a somewhat differential and to date unreported pattern for these frequency ranges in the auditory system: desynchronized beta states in task-relevant auditory regions appear to accompany the prioritization of information, but the extent of prioritization seems more level dependent for alpha.
evidence: This is a key conclusion about the differential roles of alpha and beta.

claim: Desynchronized beta states in task-relevant auditory regions appear to accompany the prioritization of information.
source: Interestingly, our results suggest a somewhat differential and to date unreported pattern for these frequency ranges in the auditory system: desynchronized beta states in task-relevant auditory regions appear to accompany the prioritization of information, but the extent of prioritization seems more level dependent for alpha.
evidence: This is a specific conclusion about the role of beta oscillations.

claim: The extent of prioritization seems more level dependent for alpha.
source: Interestingly, our results suggest a somewhat differential and to date unreported pattern for these frequency ranges in the auditory system: desynchronized beta states in task-relevant auditory regions appear to accompany the prioritization of information, but the extent of prioritization seems more level dependent for alpha.
evidence: This is a specific conclusion about the role of alpha oscillations.

claim: Illustrating a link to prioritization processes is a crucial first step in understanding the functional role of auditory cortical alpha/beta modulations during retention periods.
source: Illustrating a link to prioritization processes is a crucial first step in understanding the functional role of auditory cortical alpha/beta modulations during retention periods.
evidence: This characterizes the contribution of the current study.

claim: Prospective studies using experimental neuromodulation techniques are needed to go beyond the correlational level.
source: Prospective studies using, for example, experimental neuromodulation techniques are needed to go beyond the correlational level.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research directions.

claim: Future studies will need to test the extent to which the main direction of findings generalizes to more natural listening situations such as speech, in which the temporal features of the distractor are not predictable with absolute precision.
source: Future studies will need to test the extent to which the main direction of our findings generalizes to more natural listening situations such as speech, in which the temporal features of the distractor are not predictable with absolute precision.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research to test generalizability.

claim: Four participants were excluded because of technical issues during the testing or because the data were too noisy.
source: Four participants were excluded because of technical issues during the testing or because the data were too noisy.
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria for participants.

claim: All participants reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision and an absence of hearing problems in daily life.
source: All participants reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision and an absence of hearing problems in daily life.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for participants.

claim: None of the participants suffered or was suffering a psychological or neurological disorder.
source: None of them suffered or was suffering a psychological or neurological disorder.
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria for participants.

claim: Written informed consent was obtained from each participant before the experiment.
source: Written informed consent was obtained from each participant before the experiment.
evidence: This describes the ethical procedures followed.

claim: Participants obtained either €10/h reimbursement or credits required for their bachelor studies in psychology.
source: They obtained either €10/h reimbursement or credits required for their bachelor studies in psychology.
evidence: This describes the compensation provided to participants.

claim: All procedures were approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Salzburg.
source: All procedures were approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Salzburg.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Five head-position indicators (HPI) coils were applied (three on the forehead, and one behind each ear).
source: Five head-position indicators (HPI) coils were applied (three on the forehead, and one behind each ear).
evidence: This describes the MEG preparation procedures.

claim: Anatomical landmarks and HPI coils were recorded using a Polhemus FASTRAK digitizer.
source: Using a Polhemus FASTRAK digitizer, anatomical landmarks (nasion, left and right pre-auricular points) and HPI coils were recorded, and additionally approximately 300 head-shape points were sampled.
evidence: This describes the digitization procedure for MEG.

claim: Approximately 300 head-shape points were sampled.
source: Using a Polhemus FASTRAK digitizer, anatomical landmarks (nasion, left and right pre-auricular points) and HPI coils were recorded, and additionally approximately 300 head-shape points were sampled.
evidence: This describes the number of head-shape points digitized.

claim: Electrodes were applied horizontally and vertically to the eyes (electrooculogram).
source: To control for eye movements and heart rate, electrodes were applied horizontally and vertically to the eyes (electrooculogram), one electrode was placed on the lower left ribs and one next to the right clavicle (electrocardiogram), as well as one reference electrode on the back.
evidence: This describes the electrode placement for EOG recording.

claim: One electrode was placed on the lower left ribs and one next to the right clavicle (electrocardiogram).
source: To control for eye movements and heart rate, electrodes were applied horizontally and vertically to the eyes (electrooculogram), one electrode was placed on the lower left ribs and one next to the right clavicle (electrocardiogram), as well as one reference electrode on the back.
evidence: This describes the electrode placement for ECG recording.

claim: One reference electrode was placed on the back.
source: To control for eye movements and heart rate, electrodes were applied horizontally and vertically to the eyes (electrooculogram), one electrode was placed on the lower left ribs and one next to the right clavicle (electrocardiogram), as well as one reference electrode on the back.
evidence: This describes the reference electrode placement.

claim: A 5 min resting state was recorded, which was not utilized for the present study.
source: After entering the MEG cabin, a 5 min resting state was recorded, which was not utilized for the present study.
evidence: This describes an additional recording that was not analyzed.

claim: Visual stimuli were displayed with the PROPixx projector (VPixx Technologies Inc) on an opaque screen.
source: Visual stimuli were displayed with the PROPixx projector (VPixx Technologies Inc) on an opaque screen.
evidence: This describes the equipment used for visual stimulus presentation.

claim: Auditory stimuli were delivered using the SOUNDPixx system (VPixx Technologies Inc) through two pneumatic tubes.
source: Auditory stimuli were delivered using the SOUNDPixx system (VPixx Technologies Inc) through two pneumatic tubes.
evidence: This describes the equipment used for auditory stimulus presentation.

claim: The stimulus delay introduced by the tube was measured using a microphone (16.5 ms ± 0.1 ms).
source: The stimulus delay introduced by the tube was measured using a microphone (16.5 ms ± 0.1 ms), and this delay was taken into account and compensated for in the analysis phase.
evidence: This describes the measurement and compensation of stimulus delivery delay.

claim: The stimulus delay was taken into account and compensated for in the analysis phase.
source: The stimulus delay introduced by the tube was measured using a microphone (16.5 ms ± 0.1 ms), and this delay was taken into account and compensated for in the analysis phase.
evidence: This describes the correction applied for stimulus timing.

claim: The experiment was programmed in MATLAB 9.1 using the open source Psychophysics Toolbox.
source: The experiment was programmed in MATLAB 9.1 (The MathWorks, Natick, Massachusetts, USA) using the open source Psychophysics Toolbox (Kleiner et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the software used for experimental programming.

claim: The interstimulus interval between the presentations of the consonants was set to 1 s.
source: The interstimulus interval between the presentations of the consonants presentation was set to 1 s, and a distractor was presented to the participants 2 s after the final (fourth) letter (timepoint 1 s in Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the timing parameters of the experimental task.

claim: The scrambling of the distractor was achieved using the Matlab-based shufflewins function.
source: The scrambling of the distractor was achieved using the Matlab-based shufflewins function (Ellis, 2011).
evidence: This describes the method used to create the weak distractor.

claim: The scrambling approach preserves the frequency content of the original voice but makes it unintelligible.
source: This scrambling approach preserves the frequency content of the original voice but makes it unintelligible.
evidence: This describes the acoustic properties of the scrambled distractor.

claim: The participants were exposed to 12 blocks, six per each distractor condition and each one containing 24 trials.
source: The participants were exposed to 12 blocks, six per each distractor condition and each one containing 24 trials.
evidence: This describes the experimental design structure.

claim: An intertrial interval from 1.5 to 2.5 s (mean 2.0 s, uniformly distributed) was used.
source: An intertrial interval from 1.5 to 2.5 s (mean 2.0 s, uniformly distributed) was used.
evidence: This describes the timing between trials.

claim: One block had a duration of about 6 min.
source: One block had a duration of about 6 min.
evidence: This describes the duration of each experimental block.

claim: The sequence of the conditions and the assignment of the buttons was randomized across participants.
source: The sequence of the conditions and the assignment of the buttons was randomized across participants.
evidence: This describes the counterbalancing procedure.

claim: The brain magnetic signal was recorded at a sampling rate of 1 kHz with hardware filters of 0.1–330 Hz.
source: The brain magnetic signal was recorded (sampling rate, 1 kHz; hardware filters, 0.1–330 Hz) using a whole-head MEG device (Elekta Neuromag Triux, Elekta Oy, Finland) in a standard passive magnetically shielded room (AK3b, Vacuumschmelze, Germany).
evidence: This describes the MEG recording parameters.

claim: A whole-head MEG device (Elekta Neuromag Triux, Elekta Oy, Finland) was used for recording.
source: The brain magnetic signal was recorded (sampling rate, 1 kHz; hardware filters, 0.1–330 Hz) using a whole-head MEG device (Elekta Neuromag Triux, Elekta Oy, Finland) in a standard passive magnetically shielded room (AK3b, Vacuumschmelze, Germany).
evidence: This describes the MEG equipment used.

claim: Recording was performed in a standard passive magnetically shielded room (AK3b, Vacuumschmelze, Germany).
source: The brain magnetic signal was recorded (sampling rate, 1 kHz; hardware filters, 0.1–330 Hz) using a whole-head MEG device (Elekta Neuromag Triux, Elekta Oy, Finland) in a standard passive magnetically shielded room (AK3b, Vacuumschmelze, Germany).
evidence: This describes the recording environment.

claim: Signals were captured by 102 magnetometers and 204 orthogonally placed planar gradiometers at 102 different positions.
source: Signals were captured by 102 magnetometers and 204 orthogonally placed planar gradiometers at 102 different positions.
evidence: This describes the MEG sensor configuration.

claim: A signal space separation algorithm was used to remove external noise from the MEG signal.
source: We used a signal space separation algorithm (Taulu et al., 2005) implemented in the Maxfilter program (version 2.2.15) provided by the MEG manufacturer to remove external noise from the MEG signal (mainly 16.6 Hz, that is Austrian train AC power supply frequency, and 50 Hz plus harmonics) and to realign data to a common standard head position (to [0 0 40] mm, -trans default Maxfilter parameter) across different blocks on the basis of the measured head position at the beginning of each block.
evidence: This describes the noise reduction method used for MEG data.

claim: The signal space separation algorithm was used to realign data to a common standard head position across different blocks.
source: We used a signal space separation algorithm (Taulu et al., 2005) implemented in the Maxfilter program (version 2.2.15) provided by the MEG manufacturer to remove external noise from the MEG signal (mainly 16.6 Hz, that is Austrian train AC power supply frequency, and 50 Hz plus harmonics) and to realign data to a common standard head position (to [0 0 40] mm, -trans default Maxfilter parameter) across different blocks on the basis of the measured head position at the beginning of each block.
evidence: This describes the head position alignment procedure.

claim: A high-pass filter at 0.5 Hz (6th order zero-phase Butterworth filter) was applied to the continuous data.
source: First, a high-pass filter at 0.5 Hz (6th order zero-phase Butterworth filter) was applied to the continuous data.
evidence: This describes the filtering applied to the MEG data.

claim: Continuous data were epoched around the onset of the retention phase using a 3-s pre- and post-stimulus window.
source: Then, continuous data were epoched around the onset of the retention phase using a 3-s pre- and post-stimulus window.
evidence: This describes the epoching procedure for MEG data.

claim: For most analyses, the data were downsampled to 256 Hz.
source: For most analyses, the data were downsampled to 256 Hz (100 Hz to speed up decoding analysis, described below).
evidence: This describes the downsampling applied to the data.

claim: The epoched data were subjected to an independent component analysis (ICA) using the runica algorithm.
source: The epoched data were subjected to an independent component analysis (ICA) using the runica algorithm (Delorme and Makeig, 2004).
evidence: This describes the ICA method used for artifact removal.

claim: The Maxwell filtering greatly reduced the dimensionality of the data, from the original 306 sensors to usually 55–75 real components.
source: The Maxwell filtering greatly reduced the dimensionality of the data, from the original 306 sensors to usually 55–75 real components, depending on the single data block (Elekta Neuromag MaxFilter User's Guide, 2012).
evidence: This describes the effect of Maxwell filtering on data dimensionality.

claim: A principal components analysis (PCA) with a fixed number of components (n = 50) was performed prior to the ICA computing stage.
source: Therefore, prior to the ICA computing stage, a principal components analysis (PCA) with a fixed number of components (n = 50) was performed in order to ease the convergence of the ICA algorithm (see Demarchi et al., 2019, for example).
evidence: This describes the PCA preprocessing step before ICA.

claim: The ICA components were manually scrutinized to identify eye blinks and eye movements and to train artifact and heartbeat, resulting in approximately two to five components that were removed from the data.
source: The ICA components were manually scrutinized to identify eye blinks and eye movements and to train artifact and heartbeat, resulting in approximately two to five components that were removed from the data.
evidence: This describes the artifact identification and removal procedure.

claim: The final rank of the data ranged from 45 to 48.
source: The final rank of the data then ranged from 45 to 48.
evidence: This describes the final dimensionality of the cleaned data.

claim: Given the extensive preprocessing, no trials had to be rejected.
source: Given this extensive preprocessing, no trials had to be rejected.
evidence: This describes the outcome of the preprocessing in terms of trial retention.

claim: A five-fold cross-validation scheme was employed, stratified, repeated five times, averaging the AUC values across folds splits and repetitions.
source: For this purpose, we employed the standard settings of the MVPA toolbox, that is a five-fold cross-validation scheme (training on 230 trials, testing on 58 trial), stratified, repeated five times, averaging the AUC values across folds splits and repetitions to obtain a time-course of decoding performance (Treder, 2018).
evidence: This describes the cross-validation procedure for the decoding analysis.

claim: For the time-generalized analysis, no cross-validation was performed.
source: Note that for this latter analysis, no cross-validation was performed anymore.
evidence: This describes a methodological difference for the time-generalized analysis.

claim: A realistically shaped single-shell head model was computed by warping a template MNI brain to the participant's head shape.
source: A realistically shaped single-shell head model (Nolte, 2003) was computed by warping a template MNI brain to the participant's head shape.
evidence: This describes the head model construction for source analysis.

claim: A grid with 1 cm resolution on the template brain was morphed to fit the individual brain volume and lead fields were computed for each grid point.
source: A grid with 1 cm resolution on the template brain was morphed to fit the individual brain volume and lead fields were computed for each grid point.
evidence: This describes the source grid construction and lead field computation.

claim: LCMV spatial filters were obtained using the grid information and the covariance matrix of all sensors.
source: This information was used along with the covariance matrix of all sensors computed via the entire 30-Hz low-pass filtered epoch to obtain LCMV spatial filters (Van Veen et al., 1997).
evidence: This describes the beamformer filter computation method.

claim: Beamformer filters were multiplied with the covariance-corrected classifier weights to obtain 'informative activity' in source space.
source: These beamformer filters were subsequently multiplied with the aforementioned covariance-corrected classifier weights to obtain 'informative activity' (Marti and Dehaene, 2017) in source space (taking the absolute value on source level).
evidence: This describes the method for projecting classifier weights to source space.

claim: A permutation approach was implemented converting informative activity time series to z-values.
source: In order to make this data more interpretable, we implemented a permutation approach converting these time series to z-values and testing them across participants against 0 (see below).
evidence: This describes the statistical normalization of informative activity.

claim: Beamformer filters were used to project the single trial data onto a lSTG virtual sensor.
source: For this region, we used the beamformer filters to project the single trial data onto a lSTG virtual sensor (location of peak effect in auditory cortex across participant) and applied spectral analysis to it.
evidence: This describes the method for extracting regional activity for spectral analysis.

claim: Fourier transform of Hanning-tapered data was applied to a frequency range of 2–30 Hz (in 1 Hz steps).
source: More precisely, we used Fourier transform of Hanning-tapered data applied to a frequency range of 2–30 Hz (in 1 Hz steps) and time shifted between a period of −1.5 s to 0.5 s around onset of the distractor (shifted in steps of 0.025 s).
evidence: This describes the spectral analysis method.

claim: The time window for the spectral analysis was adapted to each frequency (four cycles).
source: The time window for the spectral analysis was adapted to each frequency (four cycles) and the analysis was performed separately for the strong and weak distractor condition.
evidence: This describes the frequency-adaptive time window for spectral analysis.

claim: Data preprocessing, spectral and source analysis was done using the Fieldtrip toolbox.
source: Data preprocessing, spectral and source analysis was done using the Fieldtrip toolbox (Oostenveld et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the software used for data analysis.

claim: For the decoding analysis, the Matlab-based open-source MVPA-Light toolbox was used.
source: For the decoding analysis, we used the Matlab-based open-source MVPA-Light toolbox (https://github.com/treder/MVPA-Light; Treder, 2019).
evidence: This describes the software used for decoding analysis.

claim: The behavioral impact of the distractor types was tested using a paired t-test.
source: The behavioral impact of the distractor types was tested using a paired t-test, comparing accuracies and reaction times.
evidence: This describes the statistical test used for behavioral data.

claim: One-tailed testing was performed for behavioral comparisons given the hypothesis that the strong distractor would be detrimental to performance.
source: Given the hypothesis that the strong distractor would be detrimental to performance, one-tailed testing was performed.
evidence: This describes the directionality of the statistical test based on the hypothesis.

claim: Randomly shuffled trial labels were generated 500 times to create a null distribution for informative activity.
source: In order to make the source projected classifier weights ('informative activity') more interpretable, we generated randomly shuffled trial labels and re-ran the same classifier and source projection approach. This was done 500 times, and the empirically observed values at each time and grid point were z-transformed using the mean and standard-deviation from the randomized data.
evidence: This describes the permutation procedure for statistical testing of informative activity.

claim: A nonparametric cluster permutation approach was employed to control for multiple comparisons, normally using 5000 randomizations.
source: To control for multiple comparisons, we employed a nonparametric cluster permutation approach as proposed by Maris and Oostenveld, 2007 normally using 5000 randomizations.
evidence: This describes the multiple comparison correction method used.

claim: Power modulations were operationalized using a log10([high power] / [low power]) ratio.
source: To this end, power modulations were operationalized using a log10([high power] / [low power]) ratio and correlated with the respective difference in the strength of memorized information.
evidence: This describes the quantification method for power modulation.

claim: Modulations of oscillations in the alpha to beta range in task-relevant sensory regions have been suggested to play an important role for functional inhibition or prioritization.
source: Modulations of oscillations in the alpha to beta range in task-relevant sensory regions have been suggested to play an important role for both mechanisms.
evidence: This is a statement about existing theoretical frameworks in the field.

claim: Regionally specific power changes around the alpha frequency range have been linked to top-down-mediated gain modulation, with enhanced power reflecting relatively inhibited states.
source: In particular, regionally specific power changes around the alpha frequency range have been linked to such a putative top-down-mediated gain modulation, with enhanced power reflecting relatively inhibited states (Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010; Klimesch et al., 2007).
evidence: This cites theoretical frameworks about the functional role of alpha oscillations.

claim: Increased alpha power in parieto-occipital cortical regions contralateral to the unattended hemifield is a very robust finding in the visual modality.
source: For example, increased alpha power in parieto-occipital cortical regions contralateral to the unattended hemifield is a very robust finding (e.g. Busch and VanRullen, 2010; Thut et al., 2006).
evidence: This cites empirical evidence from the visual attention literature.

claim: The general inhibitory gating function of localized alpha increases has been reported with respect to more specific visual features, leading to spatially circumscribed alpha modulations.
source: The general inhibitory gating function of localized alpha increases has also been reported with respect to more specific visual features, leading to remarkable spatially circumscribed alpha modulations (Jokisch and Jensen, 2007; Zumer et al., 2014) even at a retinotopic level (Popov et al., 2019).
evidence: This cites evidence for feature-specific alpha modulations in vision.

claim: Alpha increases have been reported during the retention period in the visual, somatosensory and auditory modalities, putatively protecting the to-be-remembered information against interference.
source: Also for the domain of working memory, alpha increases have been reported during the retention period in the visual (e.g. Jensen et al., 2002; Klimesch et al., 1999), somatosensory (e.g. Haegens et al., 2009) and auditory modalities (e.g. Obleser et al., 2012), putatively protecting the to-be-remembered information against interference.
evidence: This cites evidence for alpha increases in working memory across modalities.

claim: Circumscribed decreases in alpha to beta power (desynchronization) have been deemed functionally important in the context of working-memory tasks.
source: This load-dependent top-down amplification of alpha and its concomitant inhibition account are widely accepted, but circumscribed decreases in alpha to beta power (often labeled as desynchronization) have also been deemed functionally important in the context of working-memory tasks.
evidence: This describes an alternative theoretical perspective on alpha/beta power changes.

claim: In a prioritization account, alpha/beta desynchronization reflects an enhanced activation of performance-relevant neural ensembles.
source: In a prioritization account, they reflect an enhanced activation of performance-relevant neural ensembles (e.g. Noh et al., 2014; Sauseng et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the prioritization account of alpha/beta desynchronization.

claim: A framework by Hanslmayr et al., 2016 explicitly links the extent of alpha/beta desynchronization to the representational strength of the information content in episodic memory.
source: A recent framework by Hanslmayr et al., 2016 explicitly links the extent of alpha/beta desynchronization to the representational strength of the information content in episodic memory (for supportive evidence see Griffiths et al., 2019).
evidence: This cites a theoretical framework linking desynchronization to memory strength.

claim: A framework by van Ede, 2018 stresses the importance of regionally specific alpha and beta decreases when item-specific information needs to be prioritized in the retention period of working-memory tasks.
source: This is in line with a framework by van Ede, 2018 stressing the importance of regionally specific alpha and beta decreases when item-specific information needs to be prioritized in the retention period of working-memory tasks.
evidence: This cites a theoretical framework on prioritization in working memory.

claim: Temporal cues can be exploited such that when distracting sound input can be temporally predicted, inhibition or prioritization processes should be regulated in an anticipatory manner in relevant auditory regions.
source: Besides stimulus-feature information, which can influence the precise location of alpha modulations in the visual system (Popov et al., 2019), temporal cues can also be exploited (Rohenkohl and Nobre, 2011; van Ede and Chekroud, 2018): that is, when distracting sound input can be temporally predicted, inhibition or prioritization processes should be regulated in an anticipatory manner in relevant auditory regions.
evidence: This describes the theoretical prediction about temporal anticipation of distractors.

claim: An increasing amount of evidence points to a functional role of alpha oscillations in listening tasks.
source: As in other sensory modalities (Frey et al., 2015; Weisz and Obleser, 2014), an increasing amount of evidence points to a functional role of alpha oscillations in listening tasks.
evidence: This summarizes the state of evidence for alpha in auditory tasks.

claim: Increased alpha oscillations have been observed in putatively visual brain regions when focusing attention on auditory input in cue-target periods.
source: Increased alpha oscillations have been observed in putatively visual brain regions when focusing attention on auditory input in cue-target periods (Frey et al., 2014; Fu et al., 2001; Snyder and Foxe, 2010).
evidence: This cites evidence for cross-modal alpha modulation during auditory attention.

claim: A similar posterior alpha pattern is observed in challenging listening situations, for example, with increased cognitive load or when faced with background noise.
source: A similar posterior pattern is also observed in challenging listening situations, for example, with increased cognitive load or when faced with background noise (for reviews see Johnsrude and Rodd, 2016; Rönnberg et al., 2011).
evidence: This cites evidence for alpha modulation in challenging listening conditions.

claim: Increases in alpha oscillations as a mechanism for selective inhibition have rarely been shown for auditory cortex.
source: However, increases in alpha oscillations as a mechanism for selective inhibition (Strauß et al., 2014) have rarely been shown for auditory cortex, in which feature-specific processing of target and distractor sounds takes place.
evidence: This characterizes the state of evidence for alpha increases in auditory cortex.

claim: Different lines of evidence show an association between (also illusory) sound perception and low auditory cortical alpha power.
source: With regards to alpha desynchronization in auditory cortex, different lines of evidence showing an association between (also illusory) sound perception and low auditory cortical alpha power (e.g. Lange et al., 2014; Weisz et al., 2007; Weisz and Obleser, 2014; for invasive recordings illustrating sound-sensitive alpha desynchronization in anterolateral Heschl's Gyrus, see Billig et al., 2019), suggest a link to representational content as described above.
evidence: This cites evidence linking low alpha power to sound perception in auditory cortex.
